name: Microcycle
description: Given an undirected weighted graph with $$$n$$$ vertices and $$$m$$$ edges. There is at most one edge between each pair of vertices in the graph, and the graph does not contain loops (edges from a vertex to itself). The graph is not necessarily connected. A cycle in the graph is called simple if it doesn't pass through the same vertex twice and doesn't contain the same edge twice. Find any simple cycle in this graph in which the weight of the lightest edge is minimal.
input_specification: The first line of the input contains a single integer $$$t$$$ ($$$1 \le t \le 10^4$$$) — the number of test cases. Then follow the descriptions of the test cases. The first line of each test case contains two integers $$$n$$$ and $$$m$$$ ($$$3 \le n \le m \le \min(\frac{n\cdot(n - 1)}{2}, 2 \cdot 10^5)$$$) — the size of the graph and the number of edges. The next $$$m$$$ lines of the test case contain three integers $$$u$$$, $$$v$$$, and $$$w$$$ ($$$1 \le u, v \le n$$$, $$$u \ne v$$$, $$$1 \le w \le 10^6$$$) — vertices $$$u$$$ and $$$v$$$ are connected by an edge of weight $$$w$$$. It is guaranteed that there is at most one edge between each pair of vertices. Note that under the given constraints, there is always at least one simple cycle in the graph. It is guaranteed that the sum of the values of $$$m$$$ for all test cases does not exceed $$$2 \cdot 10^5$$$.
output_specification: For each test case, output a pair of numbers $$$b$$$ and $$$k$$$, where: $$$b$$$ — the minimum weight of the edge in the found cycle, $$$k$$$ — the number of vertices in the found cycle. On the next line, output $$$k$$$ numbers from $$$1$$$ to $$$n$$$  — the vertices of the cycle in traversal order. Note that the answer always exists, as under the given constraints, there is always at least one simple cycle in the graph.
approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1927F — Microcycle [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
